title: Peer Feedback & Collaborative Assessment

pts: Giving feedback requires understanding the assessment criteria deeply enough to apply them to someone else's work.
This process reinforces the giver's own understanding of the criteria at least as much as it helps the receiver.
Peer feedback is a genuine learning technique, not merely a way to reduce teacher marking load.

v: Two short learner texts on the same task; a three-item checklist

items: Learners write a short text (for example, a message inviting a friend to a school event) and put it aside.
Show three criteria on the board and check that learners understand each one.
In pairs, learners give feedback on one another’s text against the criteria.
Before hearing their partner’s comments, each learner rereads their own text and makes one change.
Partners then exchange comments and learners revise again. Ask: ‘Which change came from giving feedback, and which from receiving it?’
Use a teacher-written text for step 3, so the first round carries no social risk.
Support: criteria written as yes/no questions, with home-language glosses.
Challenge: learners add one criterion they think is missing.

blocks.x: Criteria for an invitation (written for this book):

lines: Does it say what, when and where?
Does it give a reason to come?
Does it end with a clear request for a reply?
When I read Arjun’s message I saw he did not write the time. Then I checked mine and I also forgot the time!

blocks.x: This is the effect Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found: applying criteria to someone else’s work sharpens a learner’s eye for their own.

body: Purpose: to show that feedback benefits the giver. Content: two learners at a bench exchanging papers, with arrows both ways and a lightbulb above the one giving feedback. Style: warm, simple. Board version: two stick figures, two arrows and a lightbulb.

items: Google Docs (free) with comment mode for learners who share documents.

blocks.x: Exchange notebooks across the bench; comments written on a slip clipped to the page.

pts: Give learners specific, concrete criteria to assess against — not an open 'what do you think?'
This directly extends Unit 40's presentation-feedback guidance into a general principle for all peer assessment.
Criteria checklists or simple rubrics work better than open-ended impression-sharing for genuine skill development.

v: 20 minutes to create; 10 minutes per use

items: Choose one task type (a paragraph, a short talk, a role-play).
With the class, list what a good performance looks like.
Reduce the list to three observable criteria, written as questions.
Add a line for ‘one thing that worked’ and ‘one thing to try’.
Use the same checklist for every instance of that task type across the term.
Give each learner in a group of three one criterion only, so that each listens for one thing.
Support: pictures or symbols beside each criterion.
Challenge: a simple three-level rubric (not yet, partly, fully) instead of yes/no.

lines: Open: What do you think of Priya’s paragraph? Typical answer: It is good.
Structured: Is there a topic sentence? Does every sentence support it? Is there a linking word? Typical answer: Yes, there is a topic sentence. The last sentence is about something else.

blocks.x: This generalizes the presentation checklist from Unit 40 to any task.

body: Purpose: to contrast vague and structured feedback. Content: left panel, a speech bubble filled with fog and the words ‘Nice!’; right panel, a clipboard with three ticked questions and one arrow labelled ‘try this’. Style: clean, diagrammatic. Board version: a cloud and a three-line checklist.

items: Google Forms (free) to turn the checklist into a short peer-review form.

blocks.x: Photocopied quarter-page checklists, or the checklist copied once into the back of each notebook.

pts: Model giving specific, constructive feedback explicitly before expecting learners to do it well independently.
This connects to Unit 34's point that cooperative social skills — including feedback-giving — are often not automatic.
Early peer-feedback attempts benefit from teacher modelling and gentle correction of the feedback itself.

v: A short learner text shown on the board or chart paper (with permission, or written by the teacher)

items: Show a short text and the checklist.
Think aloud as you give feedback: name the criterion, point to evidence, suggest one change.
Invite two volunteers to give feedback on a second text while the class watches.
The class comments on the feedback: was it specific, was it kind, was it useful?
Display three sentence frames for giving feedback and practise them in pairs.
Show one weak and one strong piece of feedback on the same text; learners choose the better one and explain why.
Support: frames in English and the home language side by side.
Challenge: learners give feedback without frames, then compare with the frames.

lines: I noticed that… (evidence).
This part works because…
One thing you could try is…
T: I noticed that your paragraph has three reasons. This part works because each reason has an example. One thing you could try is a linking word before the last reason, like finally.
S1: So I say ‘finally’ here?

blocks.x: As Unit 34 argued for cooperative social skills, feedback-giving is taught, not assumed.

body: Purpose: to show modelled feedback. Content: two learners in the centre giving feedback on a text, a ring of classmates around them holding small cards marked ‘specific?’, ‘kind?’, ‘useful?’. Style: lively, classroom-real. Board version: two circles inside a larger circle.

items: A document camera or phone and projector (where available) to display the text.

blocks.x: Copy the text onto chart paper in large handwriting.

body: Correct the feedback, not only the work. If a learner says Your paragraph is bad, respond with Which criterion? Show me where. Over a few weeks, learners begin to ask themselves the same question.

pts: Peer assessment complements, rather than replaces, teacher assessment — each catches different things.
This connects to Unit 21's four test qualities — peer assessment often trades some reliability for genuine formative value.
Weight peer assessment appropriately in any grading system, reflecting its formative rather than purely evaluative purpose.

v: A set of learner texts with both peer and teacher comments

items: Collect ten texts that have received peer feedback and your own feedback.
Sort the comments: content, organization, language accuracy, audience and purpose.
Note which kinds of problem peers noticed and which only you noticed.
Decide what peers will check, what you will check, and what weight (if any) peer assessment carries in grades.
Do the analysis with a colleague teaching the same grade.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Peers noticed: missing information, unclear order, a reader’s confusion (‘I didn’t understand who went’).
Only the teacher noticed: article errors, wrong verb patterns, inappropriate register.
Peers: content and organization, with the checklist. Teacher: a focused comment on one language pattern per piece.

blocks.x: In Unit 21’s terms, peer assessment trades some reliability for formative value, so it deserves little weight in summative grades and a large role in learning.

body: Purpose: to show peer and teacher assessment as complementary. Content: a learner text viewed through two magnifying glasses; one, labelled ‘Peer’, highlights meaning and organization; the other, labelled ‘Teacher’, highlights language patterns. Style: clean, symbolic. Board version: a rectangle with two circles overlapping it.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a quick tally of comment types.

blocks.x: A tally table in the teacher’s record book.

pts: Anonymous peer feedback can reduce social pressure, especially for critical feedback within a small or close-knit class.
This connects to Unit 22's classroom climate principles — feedback given carelessly can damage rapport and willingness to communicate.
Balance anonymity's psychological safety against the relationship-building value of open, attributed feedback where appropriate.

items: After a set of short talks or displayed texts, give each learner two slips.
On one slip, learners write a specific ‘star’ (something that worked) for a named classmate.
On the other, they write a ‘step’ (one thing to try), without signing it.
Stars go into one box with the writer’s name; steps go into the other anonymously.
The teacher checks the steps for tone before distributing them.
Later in the course, move to signed steps as trust grows.
Support: frames for stars and steps.
Challenge: each step must be linked to a criterion from the checklist.

lines: Star (signed): Rahul, your example about the bus stop made your point very clear. — Meena
Step (anonymous): Try to look at the class, not only at your notes.
Your talk was boring. → returned to the writer with the note: Which criterion? Rewrite as one thing to try.

blocks.x: Anonymity reduces pressure for critical comments; signed praise builds relationships (Unit 22).

body: Purpose: to show the balance of attributed and anonymous feedback. Content: two boxes on a teacher’s desk, one decorated with stars and labelled with a name tag, one plain with a question mark; slips being dropped into each. Style: friendly, uncluttered. Board version: two boxes, a star and a footprint.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) with anonymous posting enabled for steps. [VERIFY current free-plan board limit]

blocks.x: Paper slips and two cardboard boxes.

pts: Combine individual and group-level assessment components, connecting directly to Unit 34's individual-accountability principle.
Peer assessment of group contribution helps surface uneven effort that a purely product-based assessment would miss.
Use structured contribution logs or brief peer ratings rather than relying on the teacher's limited direct observation alone.

v: 5 minutes per session; 20 minutes at the end of a group project
Log sheets; a peer rating slip

items: At the start of group work, assign roles (Unit 34) and give each group a log sheet.
At the end of each session, each member writes one line: what they did today.
At the end of the project, each learner privately rates each member’s contribution on three simple criteria.
Combine a group mark for the product with an individual mark informed by the logs and ratings.
Learners divide ten tokens among members to show share of work.
Support: ratings with pictures (three faces) rather than numbers.
Challenge: learners write one sentence justifying each rating.

lines: Monday. Kavya: found two articles on water saving. Imran: wrote interview questions. Lakshmi: absent. Suresh: drew the chart.
Came prepared: 1 2 3. Did a fair share of work: 1 2 3. Helped others: 1 2 3.

blocks.x: Johnson and Johnson (1999) treat individual accountability as essential to cooperative learning. Logs and ratings surface uneven effort that a final product would hide.

body: Purpose: to show fair group assessment. Content: a finished group poster in the centre; around it, four small log sheets with names and daily entries, and a balance scale weighing ‘group product’ against ‘individual contribution’. Style: clear, even-handed. Board version: a scale with two pans.

items: Google Forms (free) for private peer ratings, one response per learner.

blocks.x: A folded rating slip handed directly to the teacher.

points.sub: Making it a habit, not an event
pts: Build peer feedback into the regular rhythm of a course, not as an occasional special activity.
Rotating feedback partners exposes learners to a wider range of work and feedback styles over a course.
This connects to Unit 19's principle that feedback loops sustain the value of any ongoing learning activity.

v: A seating plan; a rota chart

items: Choose one fixed weekly slot for peer feedback (for example, the second lesson each week).
Draw up a rota so that each learner works with a different partner every two or three weeks.
Use the same checklist format each time, changing only the criteria to match the task.
After revision, learners note one change they made because of a partner’s comment.
With fixed benches, rotate by swapping front and back benches.
Support: pair less confident learners with patient partners in the early rotations.
Challenge: confident learners review two partners’ work.

blocks.x: A rota for a class of 48 (twenty-four pairs):

lines: Weeks 1–2: bench partner. Weeks 3–4: the learner directly behind. Weeks 5–6: across the aisle. Weeks 7–8: bench partner again, to compare progress.
Zoya said my ending was too sudden, so I added a sentence about how I felt.

blocks.x: A routine slot and a ‘change I made’ note are the feedback loop of Unit 19 in action.

body: Purpose: to show rotating partners. Content: two concentric rings of learners’ initials; the inner ring turns one step each fortnight. Style: clean, schematic. Board version: two concentric circles with a few names.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a rota table.

blocks.x: A rota chart on the classroom wall.

pts: Occasionally assess the quality of the feedback given, not only the work being assessed.
This treats feedback-giving as a genuine, developing skill in its own right, worth its own attention and improvement.
Over a course, feedback quality itself becomes a visible marker of growing discourse and strategic competence.

v: A sample of anonymized peer comments; a feedback-quality checklist

items: Collect a sample of peer comments (remove names).
Share a simple checklist for good feedback: specific, linked to a criterion, kind, and actionable.
In groups, learners rate each comment against the checklist.
Groups rewrite two weak comments to make them stronger.
Each learner chooses one of their own comments from the term and improves it.
Support: pairs of comments to compare rather than rate.
Challenge: learners write a short guide to good feedback for the next year’s class.

lines: ‘Good work.’ Specific? No. Criterion? No. Kind? Yes. Actionable? No.
‘Your second paragraph has two ideas. You could split it.’ Specific? Yes. Criterion? Organization. Kind? Yes. Actionable? Yes.

blocks.x: Early comments tend to be general praise; later ones name criteria, cite evidence and suggest a next step. That shift is a visible sign of developing discourse and strategic competence (Unit 27).

body: Purpose: to show feedback quality as the final loop. Content: a circular arrow running from ‘work’ to ‘peer feedback’ to ‘revision’, with a second, smaller loop attached to ‘peer feedback’ labelled ‘feedback on feedback’. Style: clean, diagrammatic. Board version: a large circle with a smaller circle attached.

items: Mentimeter (free plan, limited questions per presentation) for a quick class vote on sample comments. [VERIFY current free-plan limits]

blocks.x: Comments written on strips and sorted into ‘strong’ and ‘needs work’ piles.

body: For one month, run peer feedback in the same weekly slot with the same checklist format. Keep every comment sheet. Then compare the first week’s comments with the last week’s.

dek: Unit 43 of 100: structured feedback between learners builds discourse and strategic competence while distributing the assessment workload beyond the teacher alone.

aims.x: Unit 8 placed peer correction as one stage in a hierarchy of feedback, and Unit 40 used peer comments to improve presentations. This unit builds peer feedback into a deliberate method in its own right.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why giving feedback develops the giver’s own understanding of quality;
design short criteria checklists that make peer feedback specific;
model and train feedback-giving as a skill in its own right;
decide how much weight peer assessment should carry in a grading plan;
manage the social risks of feedback, including when to use anonymity;
assess individual contribution to group work fairly;
build peer feedback into the regular rhythm of a course;
assess the quality of the feedback itself, not only the work.

why: Why this matters. Unit 8 introduced peer correction as one stage in an error hierarchy. This poster builds it into a fuller, more deliberate methodology in its own right.

background.x: Peer feedback is often introduced to save the teacher time, but that is not the main reason to use it. D. Royce Sadler (1989) argued that learners improve when they come to hold a concept of quality similar to the teacher’s, can compare their own work with it, and know how to close the gap. Judging a classmate’s work against shared criteria is one of the most direct ways to develop that concept. Topping’s (1998) review of peer assessment found generally positive effects, and Liu and Carless (2006) stress its learning element over its grading element.

In second language writing, the evidence points the same way. Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that university EFL learners who only gave peer feedback made greater gains in their own writing than those who only received it. Min (2006) showed that trained reviewers gave more useful comments, which partners more often took up. Hyland and Hyland (2006) summarize the wider picture: peer feedback works when it is structured, trained and combined with teacher feedback, and poorly when learners are simply told to ‘check each other’s work’.

Feedback is also social. Hattie and Timperley (2007) note that feedback aimed at the person rather than the task tends to be ineffective, and careless comments can damage the climate built in Unit 22. In many Indian classrooms learners may be reluctant to criticize a friend or a high achiever, or may feel that only the teacher has the right to judge. The NEP 2020 nonetheless calls for progress cards that include peer assessment and self-assessment alongside teacher assessment (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: para. 4.35 [VERIFY paragraph number]), and the NCF 2023 encourages collaborative learning and formative assessment (NCERT 2023). Home languages help: learners can often explain why a paragraph is unclear more precisely in Kannada, Tamil or Hindi, and the teacher can then help them say it in English.

items: Revision uptake. Compare first and second drafts to see how many peer suggestions were used, and how well.
Feedback quality. Rate a sample of each learner’s comments against the four-point feedback checklist at the start and end of term.
Group contribution. Combine product marks with contribution logs and peer ratings for an individual mark.
Learner voice. Ask: ‘Which comment from a classmate helped you most this term, and why?’
What do your learners currently do when you ask them to ‘check each other’s work’?
Which kinds of problem do peers notice well in your classes, and which do they miss?
How would you respond to a learner who says only the teacher can judge their work?
When would you choose anonymous feedback, and when signed feedback?
How fair is the way you currently assess group work?
How could home languages help learners explain what they notice in a partner’s work?

terms.def: In peer feedback, removing writers’ or reviewers’ names so that learners feel freer to give critical comments; it reduces social pressure, though signed praise can help build relationships.
The explicit qualities against which a piece of work is judged, such as task completion, organization and accuracy; sharing them with learners helps them understand what good work looks like.
A clear idea of what good work looks like, which learners need in order to judge and improve their own work (Sadler 1989); peer assessment helps develop it.
A record in which each member of a group notes what they did each week on a project, supporting fair individual assessment and accountability.
A cycle in which feedback leads to action and the result is checked, for example comment, revision and review. Without closing the loop, feedback on homework or writing has little effect.
Reviewing the quality of the feedback learners give each other, using a checklist of qualities such as specific, linked to criteria and kind, so that peer feedback improves over time.
In cooperative learning, the principle that each member is responsible for their own learning and contribution, checked for example by an individual quiz after group work.
Learners evaluating one another’s work against shared criteria; it develops their understanding of quality and supports their own learning, but needs training and clear rubrics.
Comments that learners give one another on work in progress, such as a presentation rehearsal or draft, usually guided by criteria or sentence frames.
Peer review in which learners are first taught how to give useful feedback, through modelling, criteria and practice. Training improves the quality of feedback and revisions (Min 2006).
